title: The Problem With Trump’s New Taxpayer-Funded Ads
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Your tax dollars are at work—promoting Donald Trump to the American people
In the past few days, two new ads appeared on some television channels
One, in black and white, features Trump walking down a hall and staring into the camera
In a voice-over, he says, “This is the final battle with you at my side.” The other features clips of Trump giving a speech at Mount Rushmore
But the most striking words are the ones on the bottom of the screen: Paid for by the U.S

Last week, as my colleague Matt Viser wrote , the administration aired an ad that featured images of Trump looking resolute and imposing, with the words AMERICA WILL NEVER BE A COMMUNIST COUNTRY superimposed for most of the spot, which also flashes various empty Trump policy boasts. ( Largest tax cuts in history , which is flatly false ; reigniting American manufacturing , which is dubious .) The soundtrack, apparently used without permission, is the musician JMSN’s song “Love Me.” To date, taxpayers have spent at least $443,000 on this ad alone, according to the Associated Press

The White House calls these “public service announcements,” intended only to remind “Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson told Viser
Taken at face value, this is the latest example of Trump’s Sun King–esque attempt to conflate himself and the state
This administration has named a new visa program the “Trump Gold Card,” tried to place his name before John F

Kennedy’s on an official memorial, established a 47-day training program at ICE to honor his number in the presidential sequence, printed his portrait in passports, and last week launched something called “Trump TV” under White House auspices. (It’s a glorified streaming-video app.) But the White House’s claim that these are PSAs should not be taken at face value
A much simpler term exists to describe them: propaganda

Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, pointed out that Trump’s political operation has plenty of cash to spend—almost $416 million as of August 31—and compared him to the strongman whom Hungarians toppled earlier this year: “Using taxpayer dollars, it feels like Viktor Orbán.” Another GOP senator, John Kennedy of Louisiana, said yesterday that no public official “should spend public money on private ads for themselves.” He added: “I think there oughta be a rule—well, there probably is a rule—you can’t spend public money to promote yourself.” Indeed, there is a rule
The law bars the use of taxpayer money on “publicity or propaganda.” The problem is how one defines that
The administration has cited past PSAs, including an anti-drug ad during the George W
Bush administration and a pro-COVID-vaccine spot from the Biden years, to justify the newest ads

The White House insists that these ads are not promoting Trump, because he is not currently running for election. “The PSAs are clearly not political,” an official told NBC News . “The president is not on the ballot, and the ads don’t have a call to action.” These pretexts are so skimpy that they would make a fig leaf shrivel in shame

The ads lean heavily on the White House’s big talking points this cycle, such as dark warnings about “communism.” Trump is not on the ballot, but he has repeatedly begged his supporters to treat this election as a referendum on him— writing on Truth Social this morning, “MAGA, pretend I am on the ballot.” Finally, the new ad is just a new version of one that his campaign produced late in the 2024 presidential race, only this time paid for with public money. (Perhaps someone should have edited out the line where Trump promises to “expel the warmongers from our government,” which hasn’t aged so well .) Yet just because the ads are wildly inappropriate, redolent of personalist dictators , and clearly violate the intent of the law, that doesn’t mean they can easily be stopped

A reasonable viewer will know that the ads are intended to boost Trump and Republicans in the midterms, but because the spots don’t have the “call to action” that qualifies them as campaign advocacy under the law, they may not violate the letter of the law
And even if they did, who would police that? Both houses of Congress are controlled by Republicans, whom the ad is intended to help
The Federal Election Commission doesn’t have a quorum to take action, because Trump has declined to nominate members
And anyway, the Supreme Court has consistently granted the president very wide leeway for any “official” actions
Kennedy’s there-oughta-be-a-rule response is understandable, but one big lesson of the Trump era is that writing a law to prevent every potential abuse of power is impossible
Attempting to do so would tie Congress up in reams of mind-numbing legislation
Courts might strike some of it down; other parts would be impossible to enforce; and a sufficiently motivated administration would simply find nefarious work-arounds, just as this one has
A functioning democracy cannot be just a matter of statute
It requires good faith and some measure of virtue from its officeholders
No law can substitute for character in leaders
That makes these transgressions primarily a matter for voters, not legislators or regulators
And in the case of the campaign ads, they can weigh in soon
As Paul Krugman writes , Trump’s personal unpopularity is already a drag on Republican candidates, so emphasizing his role would seem to be politically unwise
You can spend hundreds of thousands of dollars broadcasting a song called “Love me,” but you can’t make voters love you

title: A $111 Billion Hollywood Takeover With a Murky Future
excerpt: Last Thursday, during a panel discussion at The Atlantic Festival, California Attorney General Rob Bonta seemed confident that the biggest antitrust case Hollyw
body: Last Thursday, during a panel discussion at The Atlantic Festival, California Attorney General Rob Bonta seemed confident that the biggest antitrust case Hollywood has seen in decades would go his way
He told my colleague Quinta Jurecic that the coalition of 12 attorneys general who’d filed an antitrust lawsuit against the proposed Paramount–Warner Bros. merger were winning their case
The group had persuaded Paramount to not close the deal until next summer, and they’d landed a favorable trial date in March
But, Bonta said, “we are always open to coming to the table.” That seems to be exactly what happened
Last week, Paramount settled the lawsuit, ending months of negotiations
Though the agreement still has to be approved by a judge , the company has cleared its biggest hurdle to completing its $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros

The move saved Paramount plenty of cash—the company had pledged to pay Warner Bros. shareholders $7 million for each day past the end of September that the deal failed to close—while appearing to satisfy many of the requests of Bonta and his fellow attorneys general, including keeping both studios in California
Still, Bonta, at a press conference last Monday, expressed disapproval. “The settlement is not a vote of support for this merger,” he said
To misquote a classic Warner Bros. film, this seems to be the beginning of an uncomfortable friendship
Below are four reasons—all lingering questions as the merger nears its finish line

The settlement stipulates that the merged company must release at least 30 films a year for the first two years of its existence, and 32 films a year for the following three years, or pay a financial penalty

Is that number achievable? Hitting those figures could be difficult for a single, combined studio, especially because the settlement states that each year, at least four of those films must be independent productions and at least 20 of them must get a wide release (the number goes up to 21 after the first two years)
In 2025, Paramount released just eight films theatrically, while Warner Bros. released 11

The settlement also orders the new Paramount to spend $300 million more annually than it did last year to make films in the United States, rather than producing them abroad, which puts a lot of pressure on the company to generate hits, but neither Paramount nor Warner Bros. has found reliable success at the box office. (Audiences have been inconsistent in showing up to see superhero movies and legacy sequels lately; just look at the underwhelming returns on Supergirl and Practical Magic 2 .) Besides, making movies will only add to the company’s ongoing debt: Paramount borrowed more than $54 billion for its takeover bid, and because Warner Bros. already had its own debt, the combined entity owes roughly $80 billion
How will the merger affect Hollywood’s already flagging job market? Poorly, probably
Layoffs seem inevitable, considering, again, the amount of debt Paramount has gone into just to acquire Warner Bros

The settlement demands that Paramount contribute $47.5 million to a “workforce fund” over five years to aid those laid off, but giant corporate mergers have a history of massive layoffs whose costs may exceed that sum
The Disney takeover of 20th Century Fox in 2019 led to an estimated 4,000 to 10,000 slashed jobs
Consolidating Hollywood means fewer studios at which to make film and television projects, which in turn means fewer employment prospects

For now, only those at CBS News, which is owned by Paramount, appear to be relatively safe: In a settlement with the Writers Guild of America, Paramount agreed to prohibit writer layoffs there for five years
The merger brings CNN and CBS News under one roof, and under the oversight of Paramount CEO David Ellison, a Trump ally
How will that affect coverage? That’s hard to say

Some of the merger’s detractors had hoped that the antitrust lawsuit would pressure Paramount into selling off CNN as an independent enterprise, but the settlement simply states that the outlet will have an oversight committee installed to ensure its editorial independence

And though that board will consist of five journalists with at least 10 years of experience in the field and a mix of political leanings, the combined company’s board of directors, chaired by Ellison, will pick its members
Whether such an arrangement will help to prevent any corporate overreach is up in the air: To Joshua Benton, the Nieman Lab founder , the board seems like a PR move at best
After all, as Reuters noted , how the board’s decisions and findings will be implemented or enforced remains unclear
Bonta called this settlement a “strong solution that protects competition and consumers.” Is that going to turn out to be true? Again, that depends on whom you ask

California Governor Gavin Newsom, the Directors Guild of America, and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees (an organization representing more than 170,000 artists in the entertainment industry) supported settling the lawsuit to prevent further job loss
The deal at least ensures that Paramount isn’t moving out of California for the next several years, which should sustain competition among Hollywood studios to some extent

A mix of new investors could also help alleviate the extreme debt Paramount is in. (The studio’s spending could heavily influence what the new company makes for audiences to see in theaters and how much it earns in subscriptions to whatever combination HBO Max–Paramount+ streaming service.) Earlier this month, the Federal Communications Commission approved the infusion of money from foreign interests for this deal, including the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi
Semafor reported last week that Elon Musk, an Ellison and Trump ally, may be asked to invest in Paramount as well
These sources of cash would likely lead to further anxieties about how Paramount will be run, but the company has promised that its foreign investors’ stakes will involve silent, nonvoting shares
For now, the best bet on what will happen next with the merger is that the deal itself will close.

title: OpenAI Has Gone Rogue
excerpt: Over the past couple of months, a trickle of reports about AI models breaking out of their test environments and running amok on the internet have caused alarm
body: Over the past couple of months, a trickle of reports about AI models breaking out of their test environments and running amok on the internet have caused alarm inside Silicon Valley

In response to two such breaches described in early August, an AI observer noted , “If you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two.” This weekend, it became clear there is a full-blown infestation

Late last week we learned that, against OpenAI’s directives, the company’s models accessed private data in the Australian health ministry; attempted to hack or interfere with multiple U.S.-government websites; leaked private ChatGPT user data to the web; and potentially infiltrated or degraded dozens of other organizations

Then, on Saturday, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of instances of models misbehaving—circumventing internal guardrails, hijacking other websites, covertly communicating with one another
Even this might be only the start: The generative-AI industry is in the midst of an escalating crisis that it seems unable, or even unwilling, to get a handle on

And, because we are largely relying on AI companies themselves to report or confirm each incident, telling how far down the rabbit hole we already are is almost impossible. [ Read: Treat AI like a normal crisis ] When AI companies have reported their models going rogue, it has been with great delay and, frequently, under duress

Earlier this month, OpenAI published a blog post boasting about the firm’s commitment to the “value of transparency” and shared six new incidents of troubling actions taken by its AI models—most of which the company had known about since May or even April, but was telling us about only now

Google, confronted with a report that Gemini had hacked three other websites in May, confirmed the events but told The Wall Street Journal that the incidents hadn’t been serious enough to warrant public disclosure
For its part, Anthropic has said it was not reviewing for such misbehaviors until OpenAI started doing so
These delayed, sporadic disclosures make grasping the scope of the problem difficult

On Friday, OpenAI wrote that “given the scale of the review required, and the need to verify each case, this work will take months to complete.” There are “petabytes of agent activity logs” to analyze, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman added

In other words, it will take OpenAI many months more to understand events that already transpired many months ago; meanwhile, both it and Anthropic have launched new and more capable models, and Anthropic is racing toward a reported $2 trillion public offering
Perhaps more alarming than the debacles we know about are all of the presumable debacles past, and ongoing, that we aren’t aware of
Even OpenAI doesn’t even seem to have a grip on the July hack of the tech company Hugging Face that started it all

On Friday, independent researchers published findings suggesting that OpenAI agents left traces on the public web of still more nefarious actions, including trying to access Hugging Face’s internal Slack workspace
None of this was included in OpenAI’s own postmortem report
Even when OpenAI is aware of an active breach, its reaction seems lackluster, at best

Eight days ago, yet another OpenAI model gained unauthorized internet access. (This was similar to what happened in the Hugging Face hack, after which OpenAI claimed to be “adding stronger protections around future training.”) And, after noticing this latest problem, it took OpenAI two and a half hours to shut that model down due to what the firm called “operational gaps” and “confusion.” If these types of hacks were unforeseeable, maybe these companies could be forgiven—but they aren’t
Philosophers and computer scientists have for decades been imagining scenarios in which AI models, in pursuit of a goal, take catastrophic actions
OpenAI and Anthropic have both previously published research more than a year ago suggesting this sort of AI misbehavior is possible
Today’s most advanced AI systems are trained to aggressively pursue their objectives

This persistence makes the bots very effective at analyzing spreadsheets and coding, for example, but also has potentially dangerous , unintended consequences: OpenAI and Anthropic models have hacked other websites in search of answers to hard test questions, created fake personas to try to manipulate humans into doing their bidding, or attempted to upload malware to outside code bases
The AI companies that build these models know this tendency well
The fact that these problems keep recurring is, perhaps at best, plain incompetence
Or worse, it has been the plan all along: The most realistic training environment for an AI model would, after all, be reality
Employees and executives at these firms speak out endlessly about the inherent risks of what they’re building

OpenAI, Anthropic, and the like have responded in their usual way, with very serious blog posts and essays and speeches to major political bodies about how seriously the world must take the risk of generative AI

On Wednesday, the same day the Australian government shared that it had been hacked by OpenAI bots, Altman addressed the UN Security Council: “We could lose control of the future to AI,” he said. “The risk is that it moves so fast that people can no longer follow what’s happening or intervene when needed.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has written a long manifesto about the need to “pace,” or slow down, frontier-AI development, but no true public, collective effort has been made to do so
Anthropic recently said it is partnering with Accenture to perform independent evaluations of its models, although the companies also have a business partnership

OpenAI, which has a content-licensing agreement with The Atlantic , has said it is continuing to investigate and address concerning model behaviors and that, after another security incident last week, it has temporarily paused all training of its most capable models
Neither company responded to a request for comment

Rather than reining in and taking accountability for their own products, time and again these leaders fearmonger, lecture, and call on the rest of us to save us from themselves. ( The Information has reported that OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are working to create their own self-regulatory AI-safety organization.) Donald Trump, meanwhile, has scoffed at the notion of slowing AI progress, and new versions of Claude and ChatGPT keep coming
The AI industry’s tactic, as ever, has been to substitute identifying the problem for actually solving it
But at some point, you cannot blog your way out of the apocalypse
We may never fully know the scope of the AI-led hacks currently under way
What’s certain, though, is that this is still just the beginning
OpenAI and Anthropic aren’t research “labs,” as they continue to style themselves , tinkering with some new technology behind closed doors

These are mature companies offering services to hundreds of millions of people, not to mention to the world’s biggest businesses and most powerful military, based on a technology they purport to fear and evidently do not fully understand
But make no mistake: These firms have agency
It is not ChatGPT and Claude going rogue, but OpenAI and Anthropic.

title: Selections From the 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Top 100
excerpt: Veronica Donoso / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Spectacled Tyrant . “Spring is the best time to observe the spectacled tyrant in Chile, when they migrate from
body: Veronica Donoso / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Spectacled Tyrant . “Spring is the best time to observe the spectacled tyrant in Chile, when they migrate from farther north in South America
The males arrive first, followed a few weeks later by the females, who come to watch the magnificent acrobatic leaps the males perform to capture their attention
The females hop from bush to bush, searching for the best vantage point from which to observe and select a mate

Paying close attention to this behavior can yield unique moments like this one: a female spectacled tyrant at the exact moment of takeoff from a bush, spreading her wings and displaying her intense rust-colored plumage.” Fei Cheng / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Northern Pygmy-Owl . “Barely the size of a tennis ball, the northern pygmy-owl is one of the smallest owls in the world and notoriously hard to spot
My friend and I spent the day along the edge of a clear-cut forest—good hunting grounds for the owls
We carefully scanned the tree line without much success

As sunset approached and we prepared to leave, my friend noticed a small silhouette perched on a thin twig against a large trunk, briefly lit by the last golden light of the day.” Cody Cianfrance / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Mangrove Yellow Warbler . “I had never seen this many warblers in my life
Hundreds of them had gathered to feast on the abundant flies living among the mudflats
It is not often that you see a subject smaller than a warbler, so making this one seem like a giant among the flies was my goal
The hardest part was to predict when the warblers would leap from the ground into the air

Unlike large birds of prey or a wading bird that gives some indication before they take off, these warblers gave none, nor was there any pattern I could recognize before they jumped.” Dotty Doherty / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Red-Winged Blackbird . “I went to Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge to see the sandhill cranes
We birded there for three days, and on our last afternoon, we noticed a huge flock of blackbirds in the distance, but my photos showed only black silhouettes against the overcast sky
We stopped to look at cranes and ducks, and the blackbirds settled into the grasses

Two minutes later, the whole flock launched into the air, and I lay on the shutter.” Liron Gertsman / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Waved Albatross . “Española Island is the primary breeding site for the beautiful waved albatross
These majestic birds return to the island each spring to find their mate and bring life to the next generation

While visiting the island during courtship season, I witnessed this pair allopreening and mating in the sunset light.” Sergio Andrés Dueñas Trejo / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Yellow-Bellied Seedeater . “In Huila’s dry forest region, especially near farms, it is common to find dense pastures that are home to a variety of bird species
During a field trip, I noticed that in the middle of the grassland, some branches with seed heads were bending and swaying like whips

This pattern repeated in different areas, but it wasn’t until I zoomed in with my camera that I found the explanation: It was a yellow-bellied seedeater holding on to the tips of the plants and using its weight to bend them until it was hidden among the vegetation, safe from birds of prey while foraging.” Liron Gertsman / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Common Raven . “I spent a week hiking in the mountains of western Canada trying to find and photograph an elusive mountain bird, the white-tailed ptarmigan
While I did not have any success with ptarmigan, I did see common ravens, another of the few bird species that can survive winter in the high alpine environment
Ravens are impressive birds, as are the environments they live in
Toward the end of my trip, I still hadn’t captured any images I was happy with
That changed when I spotted a raven sitting in the middle of the snow with a beautiful mountain backdrop
I put on a wide-angle lens and began photographing in the freezing temperatures

As I watched, I spotted a second raven flying in and took a series of images.” Rebecca Whittaker / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards California Condor . “Hoping to photograph a California condor, I carried my gear up the High Peaks trail
I spotted a condor pair atop a pinnacle, necks entwined, distant green mountains behind them
On my way down, I witnessed the gift of a lifetime
Partly hidden, in a small pool of water, the very pair I saw earlier took turns bathing, exchanging quiet looks and gentle touches
When they finished, the female preened.” Timothy Dhalleine / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Andean Condor . “Behind this photograph lies a quiet winter day in 2022, high up in the Chilean mountains
Dozens of condors flew overhead as the wind whistled through their wings, and in my 3-year-old daughter’s eyes, I saw nothing but wonder

With a wingspan of nearly 10 feet, the Andean condor is one of the largest flying birds on the planet.” Juan David Camacho Márquez / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Scarlet-Bellied Mountain Tanager . “During the Birdwatching Tourism Congress in Manizales, I accompanied a camp for young birders and spent three wonderful days with a group that made me feel like part of a family

Together we visited the Termales del Ruiz Hotel, where we observed many amazing species, including this mountain tanager.” Harold Gillibrand Guerra / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Lesser Horned Owl . “Near the city of Coyhaique, where I live, I’ve been closely observing a pair of lesser horned owls for years
On this particular night, after waking up, the three juveniles began playing among the branches
At that moment, their father flew over the area and perched on the tallest tree
He came down with a hare he had cached there

It was fascinating to observe the hierarchy among the siblings: While the father fed the most dominant chick, the least assertive one waited patiently for its turn.” Miguel Ángel Gómez Mesa / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Rainbow-Bearded Thornbill . “I was in the field with a group of young ‘bird guardians,’ all of us united by a common goal: to learn about and catch a glimpse of one of the region’s most coveted species for birders, the rainbow-bearded thornbill
During our excursion, we were lucky enough to spot the elusive hummingbird, but it moved too fast to photograph well
But then, as the rain fell, it occurred to me that I could wait to see if it might perch somewhere—and it did
It came very close to where we were standing and then flew up to the branches in the photo.” Popayán, Cauca, Colombia

Felipe Hurtado / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Sanderling . “I was walking along Marbella Beach in Santo Domingo, hoping to enjoy the scenery and the light of the sunset, in an area where hundreds or thousands of sanderlings arrive from North America every summer

Suddenly, I saw a group flying toward me, so I took advantage of the fact that my camera was already set to a fast shutter speed and a relatively small aperture to take sunset photos—so the sun wouldn’t overexpose the image—and snapped a burst of shots.” Franco Elgueta R. / 2026 Audubon Photography Awards Stripe-Backed Bittern . “For years, I’ve visited this wetland on Chile’s central coast

title: One Reason People Are Spending So Much Time Alone
excerpt: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
body: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter

When showing up for others feels hard, some strugglers have lately steeled themselves with a version of this maxim: “Inconvenience is the cost of community.” It’s a reminder, oft-repeated on social media these days, that if you don’t want to be lonely—if you want to have robust relationships—you should occasionally do things that are effortful or even irritating, like cat sitting for a neighbor (or even just conversing with one!)
You must give up on always pursuing maximum ease
The inverse of this adage is also true: Community is, all too often, the cost of convenience

In the journalist Gabe Bullard’s new book, Against Convenience , he argues that society’s relentless pursuit of faster and more frictionless experiences carries invisible costs, and he pushes back against how unthinkingly people often accept those costs as inevitable
Some of those costs are paid in dollars, as with monthly subscription fees to Netflix rather than the onetime cost of buying a DVD
Some are paid in lowered standards: more easily accessible entertainment that’s of poorer quality (YouTube shorts, anyone?), “smart” products that become obsolete faster than their analog forebears
But in reading the book, I noticed just how many of those costs are social

Take the portability of music, which started, long before smartphones or iPods, with the introduction of the Sony Walkman, in 1979—and the headphones that came with it (which have themselves become even more portable in the decades since)

It is undeniably delightful to soundtrack your walks and bus rides with your favorite tunes, but, as Bullard writes, “isolation from others was a side effect (or a benefit, depending on your mood).” The convenience of the Walkman paved the way for a lifestyle in which Bullard can’t even hear his neighbors if they say hi, because the sound is now “among the noises canceled by my noise-canceling headphones.” Once you open your eyes to the tradeoff between convenience and community, you start seeing it everywhere
It’s more convenient to ride a Peloton bike at home alone than to go to a spin class full of other sweaty bodies (whom you might end up chatting with)
Zoom meetings make working with distant colleagues much easier, but aren’t very socially nourishing
The gig economy is rife with this bargain
Ubers and Lyfts replace rides given by friends and trips taken on public transit

Delivery replaces meals out at local restaurants and time spent in stores of all kinds. [ Read: The one line Americans (weirdly) choose to wait in ] Sometimes, the reason an innovation is even considered convenient at all is because it allows you to do something in isolation
American shoppers love it—self-checkout lines frequently thread through a store even when staffed checkouts have little to no wait
But as Bullard points out, self-checkout is more work for customers, who have to do the cashier’s job themselves

And the machines are often less efficient than human cashiers, freaking out and freezing up because you jostled an item in the bagging area. “The only effort saved,” Bullard writes, “is whatever would have gone into engaging in basic niceties with a cashier.” Similarly, recognizing an opportunity in consumers’ desire to escape the alleged inconvenience of small talk, in 2019 Uber introduced a setting to request a “quiet ride”—for an extra fee, of course
Bullard is not the first to notice the isolating effect of many innovations, nor is it just modern conveniences that take us away from other people
Against Convenience references a famous Kurt Vonnegut anecdote in which the author ignores his wife’s advice to keep a box of envelopes at home and goes out shopping every time he needs a single one

On the way, he meets people, he enjoys the scenery of the neighborhood, and he has “one hell of a good time.” “We are dancing animals,” Vonnegut wrote. “How beautiful it is to get up and go out and do something.” But sacrifices are inevitable when we pursue convenience

Many of these exchanges are clearly worth it— I keep a box of envelopes at home—but Bullard convincingly argues that the costs of convenience, social and otherwise, have crossed a worrisome threshold in the 21st century
But what does it matter if you don’t want to talk with a cashier? If you’d rather stream a movie than sit in a room full of other people? You’re only avoiding strangers, after all
For one thing, talking with strangers brings a lot of benefits
Research has found that it’s mood boosting, and often more informative than people expect
One study, called “ Mistakenly Seeking Solitude ,” found that people regularly and incorrectly assume that being alone will make them feel better than interacting with another person
Avoiding these kinds of interactions is a detriment not only to yourself but also to the society you’re part of

It is often the so-called weak ties in someone’s network—the neighbor down the block you know only casually, the barista you order a latte from once a week—who are the most important in creating a rich sense of community

Because your networks overlap only a little, your weak ties can be a bridge to new connections, or they may know about job openings and social events that you and your close ties wouldn’t have come across on your own
Without weak ties, we wouldn’t have communities, just insular cliques
In some cases, choosing a seemingly innocent convenience for yourself can create inconvenience for others

Bullard gives the example of the Starbucks app—a “smooth and inviting” interface that lets you order your drink ahead of time, with whatever customizations you want, and simply walk into a store, pick it up, and leave
But as a result, baristas’ jobs have gotten harder, due to the popularity of hypercustomized drinks that have gone viral on social media, facilitated by the ease of using the app

People would probably be less likely to order a sugar cookie iced matcha (Grande Iced Matcha Latte with oat milk, minus classic syrup, plus two pumps of sugar-cookie syrup, one pump of white mocha, vanilla-cream cold foam, and red and green sprinkles) if they had to say all of that to a person’s face and then actually watch them make it
And the proliferation of app orders means that the experience of walking into a Starbucks, and ordering and drinking your coffee there, is way more chaotic than it once was
The store is no longer a relaxing space in which to socialize, but rather “a place for fast, solitary transactions,” Bullard writes
A similar thing has happened at the many restaurants that have filled up with drivers waiting for delivery orders, crowding the diners who are there to share a meal in person
Individual conveniences add up to a deterioration of the public sphere. [ Read: Friendship, on demand ] And it isn’t just strangers whom people avoid
The preference for convenience over connection bleeds into our more intimate relationships too
Frictionless food deliveries and infinite online entertainment make it tempting to stay home alone rather than socialize—and many Americans are indeed becoming homebodies

title: How Biden Averted a War With Iran
excerpt: S hortly after Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israel, President Biden asked me to help lead negotiations for a cease-fire and hostage-release deal
body: S hortly after Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israel, President Biden asked me to help lead negotiations for a cease-fire and hostage-release deal
After some initial progress, the talks soon stalled, as fighting raged in Gaza
On February 21, 2024, I went to Cairo to restart them, carrying a new proposal
Egypt’s intelligence headquarters is in northern Cairo, surrounded by leafy avenues
Behind its gates is the heartbeat of the formidable Egyptian security state
Abbas Kamel, the head of the intelligence service from 2018 to 2024, was one of the country’s most powerful figures, although little known
A reserved man in his 60s, he had served in military intelligence with Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, now Egypt’s president, and the two had remained close ever since
Kamel was also central to the effort to stop the war in Gaza through a hostage deal
His intelligence service maintained direct channels to Hamas’s leaders in Gaza
Seated beside me in his office, Kamel lit his third cigarette and signaled to his aide Ahmed Abdel Khalek to bring the Israelis into the room. “Now!” Kamel said
Abdel Khalek skirted out the door, clutching an ever-present binder of papers
Kamel, slumped in his chair, seemed at the end of his patience
The task of delivering Hamas to a hostage deal was proving impossible
But cigarettes had a calming effect on him
The routine of sparking a lighter; the long inhale
He’d lean back, his eyes following a cloud of smoke wafting toward a fan on the ceiling
Then he’d sit up with the hint of a smile, or a new idea
Only three months earlier, Kamel and I had sat in this same room and helped close the first cease-fire deal of the war
For seven days in November, the fighting stopped
More than 100 hostages were freed—women and children, including toddlers and grandmothers—in exchange for hundreds of Palestinian prisoners held by Israel
Humanitarian aid surged into Gaza and, with the guns silent, reached those in need across the Strip
The deal collapsed when Hamas, at the last moment, refused to release the younger women it was holding
Hamas proposed that we skip over them and begin discussing the older men, a clear violation of the deal that we had put together over weeks of negotiations
This article is adapted from Brett McGurk’s new book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages
After midnight in Washington on December 1, 2023—early morning in Gaza—Hamas resumed firing rockets at Israel
At the time, I had presumed that we’d succeed in putting together another deal, at least for the remaining women and the older men, including an American citizen
They included a return to the status quo of October 6, with the organization remaining in power in Gaza, reconstituted on the borders of Israel

After the massacres of October 7, when Hamas killed more than 1,000 and took more than 250 hostages, no Israeli leader would accept that outcome. [ Mark Bowden: The lesson of Israel’s success in the air ] Let alone Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s hard-line prime minister, who demanded as a war aim that Hamas be removed from power entirely
I would see him shortly after meeting Kamel
Our talks had further stalled as Iran ramped up attacks on Americans
In Iraq and Syria, U.S. troops came under near daily fire from Iranian-backed militias
Since October 7, these attacks had increased sevenfold from the year before, and the strikes aimed to kill
On Christmas Day, three Americans were wounded in a strike in northern Iraq, one grievously
Days later, the Iranian-backed proxy in Yemen, the Houthis, opened fire against ships in the Red Sea, including U.S. military vessels
The region was on the brink of a wider war
President Biden asked me to meet the Iranians in Oman, reactivating a back channel that had been used at times before the October 7 crisis
The day before my meeting, the Houthis launched their largest attack to date, firing about two dozen missiles and drones at U.S. and U.K. military ships
On January 28, 2024, two weeks after my meeting in Oman, an Iranian-supplied drone struck the living quarters of American troops in Jordan, killing three U.S. soldiers and wounding dozens

Biden finally chose to hit back, ordering the largest wave of air strikes across Iraq and Syria in more than a decade, including targeted strikes against the militia leader responsible for the attack in Jordan and the Iranian adviser in Baghdad enabling the militias
Now, finally, we were getting back to the hostage talks

title: When can we say AI made a scientific discovery?
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here

Last Wednesday, Anthropic announced that earlier this year it had launched a molecular biology lab, where Claude agents read and conjecture about hard biology problems and human scientists run experiments on what they report

And this AI-powered lab, the company said, had made its first discovery.  To understand what Anthropic says its system did, imagine you’re flipping through a library of millions of DNA sequences, amassed as scientists sequence more and more of the living world
One step toward a breakthrough might be finding a peculiar sequence that encodes an interesting enzyme, perhaps
Then you’d need to figure out what that enzyme does and, eventually, how to manipulate it to do something useful
What Anthropic says its system of 950 agents found after 21 hours was not a brand-new sequence
The agents instead flagged a repeating pattern surrounding a known enzyme, a particular pattern Anthropic said hadn’t been catalogued before

But if you read through Anthropic’s announcement, which calls this pattern “reminiscent” of what led to the gene-editing technology CRISPR that “has already transformed science and medicine,” it sounds as if this army of agents really found something of note.  These claims have angered some biologists
A viral post from one, subsequently endorsed by the chair and CEO of the drugmaker Eli Lilly, said that “finding a weird cluster of genes and repeats is often the easy part
The hard part, and where the real discoveries come from, is figuring out what the system actually does.” The agents helped with some laboratory grunt work, in other words

But a discovery it is not.  It’s a reminder that even if AI does something impressive—like finding a pattern in a mass of biological data that would be difficult to perceive with human eyes alone—the result itself may not constitute a breakthrough for science
What is novel for AI may be routine, unsurprising, or simply not that consequential to a biologist

Muddying the issue further, Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a biologist at the University of Copenhagen, said over the weekend that his team had already discovered this particular pattern, the New York Times reported
Mestre, who regularly chatted with Claude in his work, wondered whether Anthropic’s team had learned from his conversations
Anthropic denies this, but Mestre says he’s stopping all use of Claude anyway
Part of the problem here is that AI companies aren’t presenting their systems simply as tools scientists can use, like microscopes or supercomputers
They’re insisting that the AI systems are making discoveries themselves

To some, that approach is  incompatible with how science actually works, with new knowledge more typically emerging from collaboration and an ever-growing arsenal of tools.  It’s also making people more skeptical of genuine progress when it happens
Whittling 200,000 candidates down to a few worth exploring is no small feat; it is legitimate scientific work
The fact that a general-purpose chatbot could do that work is notable, even if humans helped steer it and ultimately ran the experiments
But once the standard is whether Claude itself made a discovery, all that becomes evidence for one side or the other in a debate that has only two answers: breakthrough or bust
Once we’re judging AI by whether it has made a discovery, it’s also tempting to shift the goalposts even after it really does seem to notch a win
Earlier this month, OpenAI said its own team agents had cracked a million-dollar problem in mathematics

But a couple of weeks later, nearly every AI skeptic in my feed was sharing an article asking whether it was the math problem that really mattered .  To be clear, the piece did not argue that OpenAI’s solution was wrong
Instead, it argued that the particular result may not be the one mathematicians care most about
Throw in the accusation by a mathematician that the models may have used some of his work without credit, and people are left thinking either OpenAI cheated or the solution wasn’t important anyway
That’s part of what concerns Lucas Harrington, the biologist who wrote the post critiquing Anthropic’s announcement

He closed with a suggestion: AI companies, he said, should “set the bar high now, so that when an AI actually discovers a fundamentally new biological mechanism, everyone appreciates how big a deal it is.” But as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei race to one-up each other, raising the bar for scientific breakthroughs by AI might be the last thing on their minds.

title: Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue?
excerpt: MIT Technology Review Explains : Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next
body: MIT Technology Review Explains : Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next
Over the past few months, a cascade of cyberattacks by AI agents has stunned the world
In July, OpenAI disclosed that a swarm of its agents had escaped their sandbox and hacked into the AI platform Hugging Face to cheat on a cybersecurity test
Recently, external researchers discovered that OpenAI agents had hijacked a German wiki site and the coding platform RubyGems in May to share test answers
Earlier this month, Anthropic disclosed four incidents in which its model Claude hacked into third-party systems during cybersecurity exercises
Just last week, Google confirmed that its model Gemini had been caught hacking other companies too
The researcher who uncovered the OpenAI website hijack has warned it’s likely that similar undiscovered episodes are out there

And many say it’s only a matter of time until there’s another, possibly more damaging incident where AI agents bypass sandboxes to access systems they shouldn’t.  So the big question is: How do we hold companies liable when they lose control of their AI agents? Reporting OpenAI didn’t disclose the German wiki incident or the RubyGems incident until a group of external researchers uncovered them, and it still has not disclosed some crucial details about the Hugging Face hack
That limits our understanding of what exactly went wrong and how to prevent it from happening again

But you might be surprised to learn that OpenAI likely wasn’t legally required to disclose these incidents. (OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.) State AI transparency laws like California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’s SB 315 require that AI developers report “critical safety incidents.” These are defined as incidents that cause more than 50 deaths or physical injuries or $1 billion in damage
They also include incidents where the model deceives developers outside an evaluation in a way that materially increases catastrophic risks

Many cybersecurity incidents that don’t meet the threshold for physical damage or catastrophic risks could nonetheless be dangerous precursors to such catastrophes, and the existing laws don’t account for that. “The recent incidents are a perfect example of why the law isn’t ready,” says Mackenzie Arnold, managing director of US policy at the Institute for Law and AI, a think tank. “Only the worst, most egregious, most immediately harmful stuff is going to qualify.” With no authority under existing AI laws to demand information about anything short of a catastrophe, governments are left to borrow investigative authority from other laws or sue the companies, an expensive process that can take years.  Litigation “Normally, something like the Hugging Face incident should have been taken to court,” says Yonathan Arbel, a law professor at the University of Alabama School of Law. “Then we would have discovery, and we would have all the spillover effects that we get from litigation, where all the information comes out.”  But so far, Hugging Face has chosen not to sue OpenAI
Hugging Face’s CEO, Clément Delangue, says it doesn’t have the resources to do so (instead, he asked OpenAI for $100 million in compute)

Still, Delangue stressed in an interview with CNN at the end of July that choosing not to pursue legal action shouldn’t be taken to mean he doesn’t think OpenAI should be held accountable. “Everyone has to remember that this cyberattack is a crime
And we have to find a way to make sure these things don’t happen more regularly,” he said
Hugging Face did not respond to a request to comment
Litigation has the benefit of pushing courts to use existing laws to address AI safety incidents, rather than just waiting for new legislation
One obvious route is tort law, a body of civil law that lets people and businesses sue those who harm them

This is often used to hold companies liable for the mass harms they cause, like when families sued Boeing in 2019 over two plane crashes that killed hundreds of people, or when states and cities sued Purdue Pharma over the opioid crises, extracting settlements worth billions. “There’s plausible grounds for a negligence claim that OpenAI should have used a stronger sandbox, done more monitoring,” says Gabriel Weil, a law professor at the University of Houston Law Center
For example, when OpenAI employees discovered the covert message board that the agents had created, they could’ve promptly escalated their findings to security and safety teams

And the company could’ve better designed its sandbox to ensure that agents couldn’t access the internet.  But even if OpenAI doesn’t end up in a lawsuit over the Hugging Face hack, the threat of liability could incentivize AI labs to exercise more caution than explicitly demanded by law

OpenAI announced in its postmortem that it plans to strengthen the safeguards used to contain and monitor the models, accelerate model alignment, and improve its processes for identifying and addressing incidents.  “The liability questions raised by frontier labs’ spate of cybersecurity attacks boil down to the incentives the expectation of liability creates for their future conduct,” says Weil. “That’s why I think it’s important to get these rules right, even if the stakes are pretty low in this particular case.” Investigations One way to get answers—and determine whether OpenAI should be held liable—is to compel disclosure

But the existing state AI laws—California’s SB 53, New York’s RAISE Act, and Illinois’s 315—don’t give governments the authority to investigate incidents like the ones that happened recently.  However, amid rising public alarm, state attorneys general are stepping in, borrowing investigative powers from other laws

Alabama , Montana and a coalition of 15 other states , and California are each demanding information about the incident from OpenAI to understand whether the company’s practices violated state consumer protection laws, among others
Members of Congress are also launching their own probes

Senator Josh Hawley opened a Senate investigation earlier this month, sending OpenAI a list of questions about the incident and the company’s internal policies together with a document request, while a group of House Democrats asked OpenAI and Anthropic to release their incident logs.  “Someone needs to investigate, but it’s unfortunate that it has fallen to attorneys general, who need to rely on creative interpretations of their existing authorities to do this,” says Arnold, the US AI policy expert
Consumer protection statutes were written to catch companies that scam their customers, not companies that lose control of their software
The state attorneys general would have to show that OpenAI deceived or unfairly harmed customers, but it’s unclear if the hacking involved any such conduct
And “those [consumer protection] laws are not built for doing a thorough investigation of an AI cybersecurity incident,” says Arnold

They weren’t designed to help investigators determine whether a model was adequately contained or whether a company’s security practices were sound. “This is not the right tool for the job,” says Arbel. “The right tool would have been something like maybe a criminal investigation”—perhaps under a hacking law like the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA).  Under CFAA, hacking into another company’s computer systems without permission is a crime
But to be held liable, a hacker must have intended to break into a computer without authorization
Intent arguably requires a state of mind, and no court has ruled that AI agents have one
Without such a precedent, it’s unlikely a court would rule that AI agents had carried out a hack

Auditing One way to keep an eye on AI companies is to mandate external auditors.  After the Hugging Face hack, OpenAI brought in researchers from the AI safety nonprofits METR and Redwood Research to examine the incident

However, it constrained access to the model that led to the hacks, didn’t disclose the company’s safety and security practices, limited the length of the investigation, and had ultimate say over what the researchers could publish
We still don’t know what set the attack in motion back in May and why OpenAI’s employees who spotted the agents’ activity never escalated to their safety and security leaders

This kind of arrangement has a built-in tension: An auditor without legal authority depends on the labs’ goodwill for continued access, which means it has to scrutinize the labs without jeopardizing their relationship
Last week, Anthropic announced that the company will be hiring Accenture as an embedded evaluator to assess its models

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay that frontier AI labs should give “ongoing employee-like access” to “a team of embedded third-party evaluators (such as METR ), whose role is to verify adherence to safety practices and commitments, report incidents, and help assess the alignment of not just completed AI models but training pipelines and processes.” Most existing state AI laws do not require labs to hire an external auditor
California’s SB 53 and New York’s RAISE Act just require AI companies to publish a safety framework describing how they will test their models for dangerous capabilities and then to follow it

title: Originalism: What it is, what it isn’t and why it’s the most democratic option for the Supreme Court
url:
<title>Originalism: What it is, what it isn’t and why it’s the most democratic option for the Supreme Court</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762383/original/file-20260926-60-pw53m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3000%2C2000&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, seen here in 2006, was the court&#39;s most prominent originalist.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/supreme-court-justice-antonin-scalia-listens-to-remarks-news-photo/71149685?adppopup=true">Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The U.S. Supreme Court returns from summer break Oct. 5, 2026, and begins hearing a new year of cases.</p>

<p>Soon after what’s known as the “<a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/first-monday-october/">first Monday in October</a>” among court watchers, we will start to see stories in the media about something called “originalism.”</p>

<p>Originalism <a href="https://scholarship.law.georgetown.edu/facpub/1353/">is the judicial philosophy</a> followed by most current <a href="https://www.aei.org/commentary/misunderstanding-originalism/">Supreme Court justices</a>, but it is not well understood outside legal circles. </p>

<p>I am a law professor who worked for <a href="https://www.oyez.org/justices/antonin_scalia">the most famous originalist of them all, Justice Antonin Scalia</a>. He called originalism “<a href="https://www3.law.csuohio.edu/sites/default/files/attachment/first-assigment/6003877/scalia-originalism-the-lesser-evil-u-cinn-l-rev-1989.pdf">the lesser evil</a>.” Let me explain why.</p>

<h2>Ascendant approach</h2>

<p>Originalism is a philosophy of interpreting the U.S. Constitution. It holds that <a href="https://constitutioncenter.org/the-constitution/white-papers/on-originalism-in-constitutional-interpretation">the Constitution means whatever people reading it thought it meant</a> when it was written.</p>

<p>The opposing view is known as “<a href="https://www.law.uchicago.edu/news/living-constitution">living constitutionalism</a>.” It holds that the Constitution’s meaning can be reinterpreted by judges to keep up with the needs of the times.</p>

<p>Originalism has been around since <a href="https://no86.fedsoc.org/posts/how-long-has-originalism-been-around">the very beginning of the country</a>. But it <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108688093.002">fell out of favor during the 20th century</a>, especially after Earl Warren left the governorship of California to become the chief justice of the Supreme Court.</p>

<p>During this time, <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/2019/12/ask-the-author-the-enduring-and-controversial-legacy-of-the-warren-court/">it became popular to find new rights</a> in the Constitution that no one had previously thought were there. </p>

<p>For example, in 1973 <a href="https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-06-24/abortion-and-the-supreme-court-a-short-legal-history-of-roe">the court first recognized the constitutional right to an abortion</a>. For 200 years, laws prohibiting abortion had coexisted with the Constitution. Yet, in <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/410/113/">Roe v. Wade</a> the court held that these laws were now invalid.</p>

<p>Things began to change in 1986, when <a href="https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/archives/speech/nominations-appointments-june-17-1986">President Ronald Reagan appointed Scalia to the court</a>. He was a uniquely skilled advocate for originalism and changed many minds.</p>

<p>Today, <a href="https://www.aei.org/commentary/misunderstanding-originalism/">most of the Supreme Court justices follow originalism</a> at least to some extent, including <a href="https://lawliberty.org/the-year-in-originalism/">one of Scalia’s former law clerks, Amy Coney Barrett</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762385/original/file-20260926-50-jko7rc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman with brown hair looking pensive, with an American flag behind her." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762385/original/file-20260926-50-jko7rc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762385/original/file-20260926-50-jko7rc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=418&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762385/original/file-20260926-50-jko7rc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=418&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762385/original/file-20260926-50-jko7rc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=418&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762385/original/file-20260926-50-jko7rc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=526&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762385/original/file-20260926-50-jko7rc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=526&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762385/original/file-20260926-50-jko7rc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=526&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Myths about originalism</h2>

<p>Perhaps the most common myth about originalism is that it holds that the Constitution can never change.</p>

<p>For example, some people accuse originalists of “<a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/08/what-is-trapped-in-amber-an-originalist-explanation/">trapping the law in amber</a>.” But originalists think the Constitution can change; they just disagree with who can do the changing.</p>

<p>Originalists think the Constitution <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/originalism/">can be changed only by the American people</a> through the amendment process. Conversely, living constitutionalists believe it can be changed by judges through <a href="https://www.law.uchicago.edu/news/living-constitution">reinterpretation of the existing document</a>.</p>

<p>Another common myth is that originalism is just <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2020/04/dangers-any-non-originalist-approach-constitution/609382/">a smoke screen for conservative judges</a> to <a href="https://texaslawreview.org/selective-originalism-and-judicial-role-morality/">reach the results they personally prefer</a>. But there are plenty of examples of originalists reaching results that they personally disagreed with.</p>

<p>For example, Scalia famously <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1988/88-155">cast the deciding vote</a> in 1989 to hold unconstitutional a law criminalizing burning the American flag despite being a big patriot and despising such activities.</p>

<p>Clarence Thomas wrote in 2003 that he thought <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/539/558/#tab-opinion-1961305">laws criminalizing sodomy were “silly”</a> but could not rule that they were unconstitutional; like abortion, they had coexisted with the Constitution for hundreds of years.</p>

<p>Barrett recently said that she is <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/691090/listening-to-the-law-by-amy-coney-barrett/">morally opposed to the death penalty</a> but has no choice but to go along with it: Not only has it been around since the beginning of the country, but the Constitution explicitly says that “life” can be taken.</p>

<h2>Arguments for and against</h2>

<p>Yet originalism has many detractors.</p>

<p>Perhaps the most common criticism is that it is <a href="https://www.americanbar.org/groups/senior_lawyers/resources/voice-of-experience/2026-june/how-originalism-fails-the-rule-of-law/">often difficult to glean what people thought</a> the Constitution meant when it was written. Most of its provisions were written a long time ago, and the language is often vague.</p>

<p>In order to understand what people thought it meant, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/22/opinion/the-problems-with-originalism.html">judges need to consult history</a>. But judges are not trained as historians, and history is often ambiguous.</p>

<p>For example, sometimes we do not have a tradition of laws back to the founding of the country like we do with abortion, sodomy and the death penalty. Laws prohibiting the possession of assault weapons, for example, are of recent vintage.</p>

<p>How do you know what people hundreds of years ago would have thought about a law they didn’t have? It isn’t easy, and originalists <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/2025/12/text-and-history-not-history-and-tradition/">disagree among themselves</a> on how to figure that out.</p>

<p>But originalists say <a href="https://www3.law.csuohio.edu/sites/default/files/attachment/first-assigment/6003877/scalia-originalism-the-lesser-evil-u-cinn-l-rev-1989.pdf">everything is relative</a>: Even if originalism relies on history that will sometimes be ambiguous, what do living constitutionalists rely upon? As originalists see it, living constitutionalists rely on whatever outcome they think is a good idea. But originalists say this is undemocratic because judges are unelected and have life tenure: If the Constitution is to change, we, the people, should decide how. This is why they think history is “<a href="https://www3.law.csuohio.edu/sites/default/files/attachment/first-assigment/6003877/scalia-originalism-the-lesser-evil-u-cinn-l-rev-1989.pdf">the lesser evil</a>.”</p>



<p>Another criticism is that most of the Constitution was written when <a href="https://billofrightsinstitute.org/essays/the-history-of-voting-restrictions-and-expanding-suffrage/">Black people and women were unable to participate</a> in U.S. democracy. That leads to the question: How can originalists assert it is more democratic to rely on what people long ago thought <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/originalism">about a document that is itself undemocratic</a>?</p>

<p>This is probably the criticism of originalism that most resonates with my own students.</p>

<p><a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1109247">One response</a> given by originalists is that we have now expanded the electorate and it has since altered very little of the Constitution. Doesn’t that mean what is left is democratically legitimate?</p>

<p>Not necessarily. Because it takes a <a href="https://www.archives.gov/federal-register/constitution">supermajority of the electorate</a> to change the Constitution, it is possible that there are still provisions in place that would have never commanded majority support but fall short of supermajority opposition.</p>

<p>Again, however, originalists respond that <a href="https://www3.law.csuohio.edu/sites/default/files/attachment/first-assigment/6003877/scalia-originalism-the-lesser-evil-u-cinn-l-rev-1989.pdf">everything is relative</a>. Even if the Constitution is democratically tainted, what is the alternative? To let nine unelected judges do whatever they think is best? How is that more democratic?</p>

<p>Moreover, originalists say, even if it is possible that there are some provisions still in the Constitution that would have never been adopted with an expanded electorate, what are they? <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1109247">It may be impossible to identify them</a>.</p>

<h2>Who’s right?</h2>

<p>There is little doubt that <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/02/justice-scalia-ten-years-later/">originalism is on the rise</a> – and not only on the Supreme Court. It is increasingly popular among lower court judges, lawyers and even law professors.  </p>

<p>But as more and more people practice originalism, more and more people disagree about how to do it right.</p>

<p>In other words, originalism may be more complicated than Scalia made it sound. Moreover, even <a href="https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/how-difficult-should-the-constitution-be-to-amend">Scalia admitted</a> the amendment process is a burdensome way to incorporate change.</p>

<p>But what’s the alternative? Originalism still may be “the lesser evil.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291115/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
